issues.legal_issue: Trustees fall within the meaning of persons having an interest in a public trust.
material_facts: The temple was registered as a public trust.
The plaintiffs included the current trustee and a member of the founder’s family who was a beneficiary.
The dispute concerned property recorded as belonging to the temple and held by persons claiming adversely to the trust.
issues.conclusion: The inclusive definition of a person having an interest in a trust includes trustees as well as beneficiaries and other persons interested in the trust.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(10) of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950, as amended in 1953 by replacing “means” with “includes,” uses the expression in a generic and inclusive sense. The Court rejected the restrictive construction adopted by the Full Bench and overruled Ganapathi Ram Naik v. Kumta Shri Venkataraman Dev, I.L.R. (1963) Mys. 1059, to the extent inconsistent with this conclusion.

predicates.registered_public_trust_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a trust registered as a public trust.
predicates.claimant_is_trustee: A claimant in the proceeding holds the office of trustee of the public trust.

issues.definition: When a proceeding concerns a registered public trust and a claimant is its trustee, the trustee is treated as a person having an interest in the trust.

issues.legal_issue: Two or more persons interested in a public trust, including trustees, may use the statutory procedure to seek a declaration of trust ownership and recovery of property held adversely to the trust.
material_facts: The temple was a registered public trust, and the disputed premises were recorded as belonging to it.

The defendants had been permitted to occupy the premises in connection with services to the temple, but remained in occupation after their services ended and claimed the property adversely to the trust.
The suit sought a declaration that the property belonged to the trust and recovery of possession.
The trustee and a beneficiary joined as persons interested in the trust, and written consent to institute the suit had been obtained from the Charity Commissioner.
issues.conclusion: The suit was maintainable under section 50(ii)(a) of the Act; the Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court judgment, and decreed the plaintiffs’ suit for declaration of title, possession, and mesne profits.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 50(ii) and 50(ii)(a) of the Bombay Public Trusts Act permit the Charity Commissioner or two or more persons interested in the trust to seek, with the written consent required by section 51, a declaration that property belongs to a public trust and recovery of that property from a person holding it adversely. Section 52(1) makes sections 92 and 93 of the Code of Civil Procedure inapplicable to trusts governed by the Act. Section 50 is not in pari materia with section 92: it is wider and includes suits to preserve trust property, not only representative suits. The Court distinguished Bishwanath v. Shri Thakur Radhaballabhji, [1967] 2 S.C.R. 618, which concerned section 92 of the Code, and reversed Shree Gollaleshwar Dev v. Gangawwa Kom Shantayya Math, A.I.R. 1972 Kart. (F.B.).

predicates.public_trust_property_recovery_suit: The proceeding concerns a public trust and seeks a declaration of its ownership of property and recovery of that property from a person holding it adversely.
predicates.claimants_are_trustees_or_beneficiaries: Two or more claimants are trustees or beneficiaries of the public trust.
predicates.written_consent_obtained: The claimants obtained written consent from the authority responsible for overseeing public trusts before instituting the suit.

issues.definition: When two or more trustees or beneficiaries bring a public-trust property recovery suit after obtaining written consent, that statutory suit is maintainable.

issues.legal_issue: The statutory procedure for suits concerning public trusts does not displace a trustee’s ordinary right to sue in the name of an idol to recover trust property.
material_facts: The suit was brought in the name of the temple’s idol, represented by a trustee, to recover property said to belong to the temple.
The property was allegedly held adversely to the trust after the occupants’ permission to reside there had ended.
issues.conclusion: The statutory procedure in section 50 supplements rather than defeats the ordinary right of a manager, trustee, or shebait to bring a suit in the name of an idol to recover trust property.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 50 to 52 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act create and regulate an additional statutory right to sue; they do not extinguish the ordinary right of a manager, trustee, or shebait to sue in the usual way on behalf of an idol. The Court rejected the contrary implication drawn from section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure and distinguished Bishwanath v. Shri Thakur Radhaballabhji, [1967] 2 S.C.R. 618, because it addressed section 92 rather than the wider scheme of section 50.

predicates.public_trust_property_recovery_proceedin: The proceeding concerns recovery of property belonging to a public trust from a person holding it adversely.
predicates.trustee_sues_for_idol: A trustee brings the recovery suit in the name of the idol on whose behalf the trust property is held.

issues.definition: When a trustee sues in the name of an idol to recover public-trust property held adversely, the ordinary recovery suit remains available.
